Introduce yourself and KAVACH. The project connects login events to security alerts and makes the underlying evidence available during an investigation.

Project source: Thesis metadata.tex.

What makes suspicious logins hard to spot
A failed login has several possible causes
Someone may have mistyped a password, or the attempt may be part of repeated guessing.
An administrator needs to compare timing, failed attempts, IP addresses, and devices for the same account.
The administrator has to determine which accounts deserve attention and why.

Start with the administrator’s question: Was that failed sign-in a mistake or part of a pattern? A single record cannot answer it. Timing, repeated failures, and the account’s earlier IP and device history help the administrator decide whether to investigate.

KAVACH shows administrators which accounts need review and the login evidence behind each alert.
Six predefined rules flag patterns such as repeated failures and first-seen devices.
A rolling 24-hour score helps administrators decide which accounts to review first.
Open the linked login record and ask Grok to summarize the evidence.
Administrators use the evidence to decide whether to deactivate an account.

KAVACH addresses that problem in three steps. It flags activity using predefined rules, ranks account risk using the last 24 hours, and links alerts to the login records behind them. Grok can summarize the evidence, and an administrator can decide whether to change the account’s status.

title: Six predefined rules assign alert points

text: Six predefined rules assign alert points
One login can match several rules. Each match has its own points and severity.
A failed login brings the account to at least 5 failures in 10 minutes.
The account’s active flag is false.
The IP is unseen and at least one earlier event exists.
The device is unseen and at least one earlier event exists.
The event is marked FAILED, including an incorrect password.
Severity describes one alert. The next slide shows how points from multiple alerts combine into account risk.

The engine evaluates all six rules independently. Failed Login checks the stored FAILED status, which also applies to an inactive account’s failed event. IP and device checks compare against at least one earlier event because the current stored event is included in the history count. The brute-force description assumes chronological live login events. The repository query uses a lower cutoff only, so backdated events need separate validation.

The system assigns preset points per anomaly, then combines them into one account score.
Include each anomaly a detected for the same account in the previous 24 hours.
The score is 0 with no recent alerts. Older alerts stop contributing as the window moves.
Source: RiskService.calculateUserRisk. The 24-hour window uses the time each anomaly was detected.

First, an anomaly gets the preset points for its rule. Then RiskService sums all stored anomalies detected for the account in the preceding 24 hours. RiskService caps the result at 100. Alert severity describes an individual rule match. The risk tier describes the account’s composite score, and the score falls as old anomalies leave the window.

The composite score sets the account’s investigation priority.
Little or no recent anomaly weight.
Compare the activity with the account’s history.
The dashboard counts the account as risky.
Assess the evidence and consider quarantine.
The dashboard counts scores of 60+ as risky. The ranked watchlist shows up to 10 accounts with positive scores.

Explain the four exact boundaries. High and Critical accounts meet the dashboard Risky Accounts threshold of at least 60. The ranked watchlist is a separate query that returns up to ten users with positive recent scores in descending score order. An authorized administrator decides whether to deactivate the account. Scores indicate investigation priority.

Project source: KAVACH thesis chapters 3–5 and backend implementation.
Slide style adapted from Opportunity Engine, supplied Canva reference.
Illustrative scenario for john_doe. The account has a login history and uses a known device.
Wrong password from a new IP during off-hours.
20 failed login + 25 unusual time + 40 new IP
Same IP and device. The 5th and 6th failures overall also trigger brute force.
Starting score: 0. Both scores qualify for the Risky Accounts count. An administrator decides whether to quarantine.

Assume zero starting risk, no previous recent failures and a familiar device across all attempts. At 02:15 an incorrect password from a new IP produces 20 + 25 + 40 = 85. At 02:16 five further failures from the same IP add 5 × (20 + 25) = 225. The fifth and sixth failures overall each add 70 for brute force. The total is 85 + 225 + 140 = 450, capped at 100. The account reaches the cap as early as the next failure. The score qualifies the account for the dashboard Risky Accounts count, and an administrator can review the evidence and decide whether to quarantine it. The AI assistant can help summarize the evidence on request.

title: From Login Alert to Account Decision

text: From Login Alert to Account Decision
Example investigation · a login from an unfamiliar device
Users can review their own login history, alerts, and risk score.
Check which rule fired and open the linked login event.
Compare the event’s time, IP, and device with earlier logins.
Deactivate the account if the evidence warrants it. The audit trail records the action.

Explain the role difference first. A user can check their own login history, alerts and risk. An administrator can review alerts across accounts. For a new-device alert, open the linked login record, compare the device and other details with the account’s history, and decide whether to deactivate the account. Account changes are recorded in the audit trail, and administrators can reactivate the account when appropriate.
